metadata.title: Solving Composite Monotone Inclusions in Reflexive Banach Spaces by Constructing Best Bregman Approximations from Their Kuhn-Tucker Set

extraction_notes.note: The iterations (3.2) and (3.50) are numbered equations, but the paper calls them 'algorithm (3.2)' and they are array-formatted pseudocode; typed as algorithm (confidence 0.9) with unmarked algorithm_step children rather than equation.
Proofs are organized by item labels written as '\ref{item}:' paragraph openers, which latex_facts does not report as labels; treated them as author labels (step confidence 0.95).
Remark 3.4 is essentially a worked example (explicit Bregman resolvent in R^2); kept as remark per its environment.
Motivational prose (history of splitting methods, Haugazeau's algorithm, the comparison with Moreau's proximity operator before Example 4.3) was not turned into nodes.

Set $\boldsymbol{M}\colon\boldsymbol{\mathcal{X}}\to
2^{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{X}}^*}\colon(x,y^*)\mapsto 
Ax\times B^{-1}y^*$ and
$\boldsymbol{S}\colon\boldsymbol{\mathcal{X}}
\to\boldsymbol{\mathcal{X}}^*\colon (x,y^*)\mapsto (L^*y^*,-Lx)$.
Since $A$ and $B^{-1}$ are maximally monotone, so is 
$\boldsymbol{M}$. On the other hand, $\boldsymbol{S}$ is linear, 
bounded, and positive since 
\begin{equation}
\label{egVxZ5y821}
(\forall(x,y^*)\in\ensuremath{\boldsymbol{\mathcal X}})\quad
\pair{\boldsymbol{S}(x,y^*)}{(x,y^*)}=
\pair{x}{L^*y^*}+\pair{-Lx}{y^*}=0. 
\end{equation}
Thus, it follows from \cite[Section~17]{Simo08} that 
$\boldsymbol{S}$ is maximally monotone with 
$\ensuremath{\text{\rm dom}\,}\boldsymbol{S}=\ensuremath{\boldsymbol{\mathcal X}}$. In turn, we derive from 
\cite[Theorem~24.1(a)]{Simo08} that
\begin{equation}
\label{egVxZ5y820}
\boldsymbol{M}+\boldsymbol{S}\;\text{is maximally monotone.}
\end{equation}

\ref{ppOlk28ha12ia}:
Let $(x,y^*)\in\ensuremath{\boldsymbol{\mathcal X}}$. Then
\begin{eqnarray}
\label{egVxZ5y828}
\boldsymbol{0}\in\boldsymbol{M}(x,y^*)+\boldsymbol{S}(x,y^*)
&\Leftrightarrow& 0\in Ax+L^*y^*\quad\text{and}\quad 0\in 
B^{-1}y^*-Lx\nonumber\\
&\Leftrightarrow& -L^*y^*\in Ax
\quad\text{and}\quad Lx\in B^{-1}y^*\nonumber\\
&\Leftrightarrow& (x,y^*)\in \boldsymbol{Z}.
\end{eqnarray}
Therefore, we derive from \eqref{egVxZ5y820} and
\cite[Lemma~1.1(a)]{IVBro65} that
$\boldsymbol{Z}=\ensuremath{\text{\rm zer}\,}(\boldsymbol{M}+\boldsymbol{S})=
(\boldsymbol{M}+\boldsymbol{S})^{-1}(0)$ is closed and convex.

\ref{ppOlk28ha12ib}: Let $x\in\ensuremath{{\mathcal X}}$. Then
$x\in\mathscr{P}\Leftrightarrow
0\in Ax+L^*BLx\Leftrightarrow (\ensuremath{\exists\,} y^*\in\ensuremath{{\mathcal Y}}^*)\; 
[-L^*y^*\in Ax\;\text{and}\;y^*\in BLx]
\Leftrightarrow (\ensuremath{\exists\,} y^*\in\ensuremath{{\mathcal Y}}^*)\;(x,y^*)
\in\boldsymbol{Z}$. 
Hence $\mathscr{P}\neq\ensuremath{{\varnothing}}$
$\Leftrightarrow$ $\boldsymbol{Z}\neq\ensuremath{{\varnothing}}$.
Likewise, let $y^*\in\ensuremath{{\mathcal Y}}^*$. Then 
$y^*\in\mathscr{D}\Leftrightarrow
0\in-LA^{-1}(-L^*y^*)+B^{-1}y^*
\Leftrightarrow(\ensuremath{\exists\,} x\in\ensuremath{{\mathcal X}})\; 
[x\in A^{-1}(-L^*y^*)\;\text{and}\;0\in-Lx+B^{-1}y^*]
\Leftrightarrow(\ensuremath{\exists\,} x\in\ensuremath{{\mathcal X}})\; 
[-L^*y^*\in Ax\;\text{and}\; Lx\in B^{-1}y^*]
\Leftrightarrow(\ensuremath{\exists\,} x\in\ensuremath{{\mathcal X}})\;(x,y^*)\in\boldsymbol{Z}$.

\ref{ppOlk28ha12ic}: Clear from \ref{ppOlk28ha12ib} (see also
\cite[Corollary 2.4]{IVPe00}).

and $\ensuremath{\text{\rm dom}\,}\partial g^*=\ensuremath{\text{\rm int\,dom}\,} g^*$, respectively. 
On the other hand, we derive from \eqref{epOlk28ha14} that 
$\ensuremath{\text{\rm dom}\,}\boldsymbol{f}=\ensuremath{\text{\rm dom}\,} f\times\ensuremath{\text{\rm dom}\,} g^*$ and that
\begin{equation}

2^{\boldsymbol{\ensuremath{{\mathcal X}}^*}}\colon (x,y^*)\mapsto

We first observe that \cite[Theorem~18.7]{Simo08} and 
\cite[Theorem~5.6]{Ccm01} imply that $\nabla h$ is maximally 
monotone and that $\ensuremath{\text{\rm dom}\,}\nabla h=\ensuremath{\text{\rm int\,dom}\,} h$.

\ref{IVcl:20b1}: Lemma~\ref{l:20}\ref{l:20i}.

\ref{IVcl:20b2}: 
It follows from Lemma~\ref{IVlhHg7yG02} that
$\nabla h+M$ is coercive. 

\ref{IVcl:20b3}: Since $\nabla h+M$ is uniformly monotone at $z$ 
with a supercoercive modulus, the claim follows from 
Lemma~\ref{l:20}\ref{l:20ii}.

\ref{IVcl:20b4}: 
Let $z\in\ensuremath{\text{\rm dom}\,} M\cap\ensuremath{\text{\rm int\,dom}\,} h=\ensuremath{\text{\rm dom}\,} M\cap\ensuremath{\text{\rm dom}\,}\partial h$. 
Then we derive from 
\eqref{eQA8h34-06} that 
\begin{equation}
\lim_{\|x\|\to+\infty}\dfrac{\pair{x-z}{\nabla h(x)}}{\|x\|}=\ensuremath{{+\infty}}.
\end{equation}
Thus, $\nabla h$ satisfies \eqref{e:M1} and it follows from 
Lemma~\ref{IVlhHg7yG02} that $\nabla h+M$ is coercive. 

\ref{IVcl:20b5}: It follows from 
\cite[Definition~2.2 and Remark~2.8]{IVZali83} that $\nabla h$ is
uniformly monotone at $z$ with a supercoercive modulus. Hence, 
$\nabla h+M$ is likewise and Lemma~\ref{l:20}\ref{l:20ii} implies 
that $\nabla h+M$ is coercive. Alternatively, this is a special
case of \ref{IVcl:20b4}.

Finally, suppose that $M$ is maximally monotone. Then 
\cite[Theorem~24.1(a)]{Simo08} asserts that $\nabla h+M$ is 
maximally monotone. Consequently, since $\nabla h+M$ is 
coercive, it follows from 
\cite[Corollary~II-B.32.35]{ZeidXX} that

We provide a couple of settings that satisfy the assumptions of
Theorem~\ref{IVt:1}.
\begin{enumerate}
\item
In Problem~\ref{prob:1}, suppose that $\ensuremath{{\mathcal X}}$ and $\ensuremath{{\mathcal Y}}$ are Hilbert 
spaces, that $f=\|\cdot\|^2/2$, and that $g=\|\cdot\|^2/2$.
Furthermore, in Theorem~\ref{IVt:1}, set $h=f$ and $j=g$, and note
that, for any $\varepsilon\in\ensuremath{\left]0,+\infty\right[}$, 
$\nabla h+\varepsilon A=\ensuremath{\operatorname{Id}}\,+\varepsilon A$ and 
$\nabla j+\varepsilon B=\ensuremath{\operatorname{Id}}\,+\varepsilon B$ are strongly monotone 
and hence coercive by Lemma~\ref{l:20}\ref{l:20ii}.
Then we recover the framework of \cite{Nfao15}, 
which has been applied to domain decomposition problems in 
\cite{Atto15}. 
\item
Let $(\Omega_1,\mathcal{F}_1,\mu_1)$ and
$(\Omega_2,\mathcal{F}_2,\mu_2)$ be measure spaces,
let $p$ and $q$ be in $\left]1,\ensuremath{{+\infty}}\right[$, and set
$p^*=p/(p-1)$ and $q^*=q/(q-1)$. In Problem~\ref{prob:1}, suppose 
that $\ensuremath{{\mathcal X}}=L^p(\Omega_1,\mathcal{F}_1,\mu_1)$, 
$\ensuremath{{\mathcal Y}}=L^q(\Omega_2,\mathcal{F}_2,\mu_2)$, $f=\|\cdot\|^p/p$, 
and $g=\|\cdot\|^q/q$. Then
$\ensuremath{{\mathcal X}}^*=L^{p^*}(\Omega_1,\mathcal{F}_1,\mu_1)$,
$\ensuremath{{\mathcal Y}}^*=L^{q^*}(\Omega_2,\mathcal{F}_2,\mu_2)$, and
$g^*=\|\cdot\|^{q^*}/q^*$. Moreover, 
it follows from Clarkson's theorem 
\cite[Theorem~II.4.7]{IVCi90_B} that $\ensuremath{{\mathcal X}}$, $\ensuremath{{\mathcal X}}^*$,
$\ensuremath{{\mathcal Y}}$, and $\ensuremath{{\mathcal Y}}^*$ are uniformly convex and uniformly smooth.
Hence, we derive from \cite[Corollary~5.5 and Example~6.5]{Ccm01} 
that $f$, $g$, and $g^*$ are Legendre functions which are 
uniformly convex on every bounded set, and which therefore 
satisfy Condition~\ref{IVC:1} by virtue of 
\cite[Example~4.10(i)]{Sico03}. 
Now set $h=f$ and $j=g$ in Theorem~\ref{IVt:1}.
We derive from 
\cite[Theorem~II.2.16(i)]{IVCi90_B} that $\nabla h$ and $\nabla j$ 
are uniformly continuous on every bounded subset of $\ensuremath{{\mathcal X}}$ and 
$\ensuremath{{\mathcal Y}}$, respectively. 
In addition, $h$ and $j$ are supercoercive and therefore,
for any $\varepsilon\in\ensuremath{\left]0,+\infty\right[}$, 
Proposition~\ref{IVpp:20a}\ref{IVcl:20b4} asserts that 
$\nabla h+\varepsilon A$ and $\nabla j+\varepsilon B$ are 
coercive. Finally, it follows from 
\cite[Proposition~II.4.9]{IVCi90_B} that
$\nabla h\colon x\mapsto |x|^{p-1}\ensuremath{\text{\rm sign}}(x)$ and 
$\nabla j\colon y\mapsto |y|^{q-1}\ensuremath{\text{\rm sign}}(y)$.
\end{enumerate}

The implementation of algorithm \eqref{IVe:Bfg+uh4f9-09h}
requires the evaluation of the operator $(\nabla h+A)^{-1}$.
We provide a simple example in the Euclidean plane $\ensuremath{{\mathcal X}}$ of a
maximally monotone operator $A$ for which 
$(\nabla h+A)^{-1}$ can be computed explicitly, whereas
the classical resolvent $(\ensuremath{\operatorname{Id}}\,+A)^{-1}$ is difficult to evaluate.
Let $\beta\in\ensuremath{\left]0,+\infty\right[}$ and let $\psi\colon\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}\to\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}$ be a Legendre 
function with a $\beta$ Lipschitz-continuous derivative.
Set
\begin{equation}
A\colon\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^2\to\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^2\colon (\xi_1,\xi_2)\mapsto
\big(\beta\xi_1-\psi'(\xi_1)-\xi_2,
\xi_1+\beta\xi_2-\psi'(\xi_2)\big)
\end{equation}
and 
\begin{equation}
h\colon\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^2\to\ensuremath{\left]-\infty,+\infty\right]}\colon (\xi_1,\xi_2)\mapsto
\psi(\xi_1)+\psi(\xi_2).
\end{equation}
Then it follows from \cite[Theorem~18.15]{Livre1} that $A$ is the
sum of the gradient of the convex function 
$(\xi_1,\xi_2)\mapsto\beta\xi_1^2/2-\psi(\xi_1)+
\beta\xi_2^2/2-\psi(\xi_2)$ 
and of the skew linear operator $(\xi_1,\xi_2)\mapsto(-\xi_2,\xi_1)$.
Thus, $A$ is a maximally monotone operator 
\cite[Corollary~24.4]{Livre1} which is not the
subdifferential of a convex function. In addition, as in 
Proposition~\ref{pvb8uh4504}\ref{pvb8uh4504i},
$h$ is a Legendre function and
\begin{equation}
\big(\forall (\xi_1,\xi_2)\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^2\big)\quad 
(\nabla h+A)^{-1}(\xi_1,\xi_2)
=\Bigg(\dfrac{\beta\xi_1+\xi_2}{1+\beta^2},
\dfrac{\beta\xi_2-\xi_1}{1+\beta^2}\Bigg).
\end{equation}

\begin{proposition}
\label{4p:1}
Consider the setting of Problem~\ref{IVpb:V3}. For every 
$i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$, let $h_i\in\Gamma_0(\ensuremath{{\mathcal X}}_i)$ be a Legendre 
function such that $\ensuremath{\text{\rm int\,dom}\,} f_i\subset\ensuremath{\text{\rm int\,dom}\,} h_i$ and 
$h_i+\varepsilon_i\varphi_i$ is supercoercive for some
$\varepsilon_i\in\ensuremath{\left]0,+\infty\right[}$.
For every $k\in\{1,\ldots,p\}$, let $j_k\in\Gamma_0(\ensuremath{{\mathcal Y}}_k)$ 
be a Legendre function such that 
$\sum_{i=1}^mL_{ki}(\ensuremath{\text{\rm int\,dom}\,} f_i)\subset\ensuremath{\text{\rm int\,dom}\,} j_k$ and 
$j_k+\delta_k\psi_k$ is supercoercive for some $\delta_k\in\ensuremath{\left]0,+\infty\right[}$. 
Set $\varepsilon=\max_{1\ensuremath{\leqslant} i\ensuremath{\leqslant} m}\varepsilon_i$ and
$\delta=\max_{1\ensuremath{\leqslant} k\ensuremath{\leqslant} p}\delta_k$, let 
$\sigma\in\left[\max\{\varepsilon,\delta\},+\infty\right[$, and 
iterate
\begin{equation}
\label{4eKKnhf74g203}
\begin{array}{l}
\text{for}\;n=0,1,\ldots\\
\left\lfloor
\begin{array}{l}
(\gamma_n,\mu_n)\in\left[\varepsilon,\sigma\right]
\times\left[\delta,\sigma\right]\\[1mm]
\text{for}\;i=1,\ldots,m\\
\left\lfloor
\begin{array}{l}
a_{i,n}=(\nabla h_i+\gamma_n\partial\varphi_i)^{-1}
\Big(\nabla h_i(x_{i,n})
-\gamma_n\sum_{k=1}^pL_{ki}^*y_{k,n}^*\Big)\\[2mm]
a_{i,n}^*=\gamma_n^{-1}\big(\nabla h_i(x_{i,n})
-\nabla h_i(a_{i,n})\big)-\sum_{k=1}^pL_{ki}^*y_{k,n}^*\\[1mm]
\end{array}
\right.\\[3mm]
\text{for}\;k=1,\ldots,p\\
\left\lfloor
\begin{array}{l}
b_{k,n}=(\nabla j_k+\mu_n\partial\psi_k)^{-1}
\big(\nabla j_k\big(\sum_{i=1}^mL_{ki}x_{i,n}\big)
+\mu_ny_{k,n}^*\big)\\[1mm]
b_{k,n}^*=\mu_n^{-1}\big(\nabla j_k\big(\sum_{i=1}^m
L_{ki}x_{i,n}\big)-\nabla j_k(b_{k,n})\big)+y_{k,n}^*\\[1mm]
t_{k,n}=b_{k,n}-\sum_{i=1}^mL_{ki}a_{i,n}\\[1mm]
\end{array}
\right.\\
\text{for}\;i=1,\ldots,m\\
\left\lfloor
\begin{array}{l}
s_{i,n}^*=a_{i,n}^*+\sum_{k=1}^pL_{ki}^*b_{k,n}^*\\[1mm]
\end{array}
\right.\\
\eta_n=\sum_{i=1}^m\pair{a_{i,n}}{a_{i,n}^*}
+\sum_{k=1}^p\pair{b_{k,n}}{b_{k,n}^*}\\[1mm]
\boldsymbol{H}_n=
\Menge{({x},{y}^*)\in\ensuremath{\boldsymbol{\mathcal X}}}
{\sum_{i=1}^m\pair{x_i}{s_{i,n}^*}
+\sum_{k=1}^p\pair{t_{k,n}}{y_k^*}
\ensuremath{\leqslant}\eta_n}\\[1mm]
\big({x}_{n+1/2},{y}_{n+1/2}^*\big)
=P^{\boldsymbol{f}}_{\boldsymbol{H}_n}
({x}_n,{y}^*_n)\\[1mm]
\big({x}_{n+1},{y}_{n+1}^*\big)=
Q^{{f}}\big(({x}_0,{y}_0^*),
({x}_n,{y}^*_n),
({x}_{n+1/2},{y}_{n+1/2}^*)\big),\\[1mm]
\end{array}
\right.\\
\end{array}
\end{equation}
where we use the notation $(\forall n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb N})$ 
$x_n=(x_{i,n})_{1\ensuremath{\leqslant} i\ensuremath{\leqslant} m}$ and
$y^*_n=(y^*_{k,n})_{1\ensuremath{\leqslant} k\ensuremath{\leqslant} p}$. 
Suppose that the following hold: 
\begin{enumerate}
\item
For every $i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$, $f_i$ and $h_i$ satisfy 
Condition~\ref{IVC:1} and $\nabla h_i$ is uniformly continuous on 
every bounded subset of $\ensuremath{\text{\rm int}\,}\ensuremath{\text{\rm dom}\,} h_i$.
\item
For every $k\in\{1,\ldots,p\}$, $g_k^*$ and $j_k$ satisfy 
Condition~\ref{IVC:1} and $\nabla j_k$ is uniformly continuous on 
every bounded subset of $\ensuremath{\text{\rm int}\,}\ensuremath{\text{\rm dom}\,} j_k$.
\end{enumerate}
Then 
\begin{equation}
(\forall i\in\{1,\ldots,m\})\quad 
x_{i,n}\to\overline{x}_i
\quad\text{and}\quad 
(\forall k\in\{1,\ldots,p\})\quad 
y_{k,n}^*\to\overline{y}_k^*.
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Denote by $\ensuremath{{\mathcal X}}$ and $\ensuremath{{\mathcal Y}}$ the standard vector product spaces 
$\ensuremath{\raisebox{-0.5mm}{\mbox{\huge{$\times$}}}}_{\!\!i=1}^{\!\!m}\ensuremath{{\mathcal X}}_i$ and 
$\ensuremath{\raisebox{-0.5mm}{\mbox{\huge{$\times$}}}}_{\!\!k=1}^{\!\!p}\ensuremath{{\mathcal Y}}_k$ equipped with the norms 
$x=(x_i)_{1\ensuremath{\leqslant} i\ensuremath{\leqslant} m}\mapsto\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^m\|x_i\|^2}$ and 
$y=(y_k)_{1\ensuremath{\leqslant} k\ensuremath{\leqslant} p}\mapsto\sqrt{\sum_{k=1}^p\|y_k\|^2}$,
respectively. Then $\ensuremath{{\mathcal X}}^*$ is the vector product space 
$\ensuremath{\raisebox{-0.5mm}{\mbox{\huge{$\times$}}}}_{\!\!i=1}^{\!\!m}\ensuremath{{\mathcal X}}_i^*$ equipped with the norm 
$x^*\mapsto\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^m\|x_i^*\|^2}$ 
and $\ensuremath{{\mathcal Y}}^*$ is the vector product space 
$\ensuremath{\raisebox{-0.5mm}{\mbox{\huge{$\times$}}}}_{\!\!k=1}^{\!\!p}\ensuremath{{\mathcal Y}}_k^*$ equipped with the norm 
$y^*\mapsto\sqrt{\sum_{k=1}^p\|y_k^*\|^2}$. 
Let us introduce the operators
\begin{equation}
\label{4e:opt1}
\begin{cases}
A\colon\ensuremath{{\mathcal X}}\to 2^{\ensuremath{{\mathcal X}}^*}\colon x\mapsto
\ensuremath{\raisebox{-0.5mm}{\mbox{\huge{$\times$}}}}_{\!\!i=1}^{\!\!m}\partial\varphi_i(x_i)\\
B\colon\ensuremath{{\mathcal Y}}\to 2^{\ensuremath{{\mathcal Y}}^*}\colon y
\mapsto\ensuremath{\raisebox{-0.5mm}{\mbox{\huge{$\times$}}}}_{\!\!k=1}^{\!\!p}\partial\psi_k(y_k)\\
L\colon\ensuremath{{\mathcal X}}\to\ensuremath{{\mathcal Y}}\colon x\mapsto
\big(\sum_{i=1}^mL_{ki}x_i\big)_{1\ensuremath{\leqslant} k\ensuremath{\leqslant} p}
\end{cases}
\end{equation}
and the functions
\begin{equation}
\label{4e:funct1}
\begin{cases}
f\colon\ensuremath{{\mathcal X}}\to\ensuremath{\left]-\infty,+\infty\right]}\colon x\mapsto\sum_{i=1}^mf_i(x_i)\\
h\colon\ensuremath{{\mathcal X}}\to\ensuremath{\left]-\infty,+\infty\right]}\colon x\mapsto\sum_{i=1}^mh_i(x_i)\\
\varphi\colon\ensuremath{{\mathcal X}}\to\ensuremath{\left]-\infty,+\infty\right]}\colon x\mapsto\sum_{i=1}^m\varphi_i(x_i)\\
g\colon\ensuremath{{\mathcal Y}}\to\ensuremath{\left]-\infty,+\infty\right]}\colon y\mapsto\sum_{k=1}^pg_k(y_k)\\
j\colon\ensuremath{{\mathcal Y}}\to\ensuremath{\left]-\infty,+\infty\right]}\colon y\mapsto\sum_{k=1}^pj_k(y_k).
\end{cases}
\end{equation}
Then it follows from \cite[Theorem~3.1.11]{IVZali02} that $A$ 
and $B$ are maximally monotone. In addition, the adjoint of $L$ is 
$L^*\colon\ensuremath{{\mathcal Y}}^*\to\ensuremath{{\mathcal X}}^*\colon y^*\mapsto(\sum_{k=1}^p
L_{ki}^*y_k^*)_{1\ensuremath{\leqslant} i\ensuremath{\leqslant} m}$, and, as in
Proposition~\ref{pvb8uh4504}\ref{pvb8uh4504i},
$f$ and $g$ are Legendre functions. 
Thus, Problem~\ref{IVpb:V3} is a special case of 
Problem~\ref{prob:1}. Furthermore, $h$ and $j$ are Legendre
functions,
\begin{equation}
\label{ekIuh711a}
\ensuremath{\text{\rm int\,dom}\,} f=\underset{i=1}{\overset{m}{\ensuremath{\raisebox{-0.5mm}{\mbox{\huge{$\times$}}}}}}\ensuremath{\text{\rm int}\,}\ensuremath{\text{\rm dom}\,} f_i\subset
\underset{i=1}{\overset{m}{\ensuremath{\raisebox{-0.5mm}{\mbox{\huge{$\times$}}}}}}\ensuremath{\text{\rm int}\,}\ensuremath{\text{\rm dom}\,} h_i=\ensuremath{\text{\rm int\,dom}\,} h,
\end{equation}
and 
\begin{equation}
\label{ekIuh711b}
L\big(\ensuremath{\text{\rm int\,dom}\,} f\big)=\underset{k=1}{\overset{p}{\ensuremath{\raisebox{-0.5mm}{\mbox{\huge{$\times$}}}}}}
\sum_{i=1}^m L_{ki}(\ensuremath{\text{\rm int\,dom}\,} f_i)\subset
\underset{k=1}{\overset{p}{\ensuremath{\raisebox{-0.5mm}{\mbox{\huge{$\times$}}}}}}\ensuremath{\text{\rm int}\,}\ensuremath{\text{\rm dom}\,} j_k=\ensuremath{\text{\rm int\,dom}\,} j.
\end{equation}
Next we observe that, for every $i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$, since 
$h_i+\varepsilon\varphi_i$ is supercoercive, 
$(h_i+\varepsilon\varphi_i)^*$ is bounded above on
every bounded subset of $\ensuremath{{\mathcal X}}_i^*$ \cite[Theorem~3.3]{Ccm01}.
As a result, 
$(h+\varepsilon\varphi)^*\colon x^*\mapsto\sum_{i=1}^m
(h_i+\varepsilon\varphi_i)^*(x_i^*)$ 
is bounded above on every bounded subset of $\ensuremath{{\mathcal X}}^*$, and it follows
from \cite[Theorem~3.3]{Ccm01} that $h+\varepsilon\varphi$ is
supercoercive. In turn since, as in \eqref{ehHg7yG10a},
$\ensuremath{{\varnothing}}\neq\ensuremath{\text{\rm dom}\,} A\cap\ensuremath{\text{\rm int\,dom}\,} f\subset
\ensuremath{\text{\rm dom}\,}\varphi\cap\ensuremath{\text{\rm int\,dom}\,} f$, we derive from 
\cite[Theorem~2.8.3]{IVZali02}
and Lemma~\ref{l:20}\ref{l:20iii} that
\begin{equation}
\label{ekIuh713}
\nabla h+\varepsilon A=\nabla h+\varepsilon\partial\varphi=
\partial(h+\varepsilon\varphi) 
\end{equation}
is coercive. We show in a similar fashion that $\nabla j+\delta B$ 
is coercive. Now set, for every $n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb N}$, 
$a_n=(a_{i,n})_{1\ensuremath{\leqslant} i\ensuremath{\leqslant} m}$, 
$a_n^*=(a_{i,n}^*)_{1\ensuremath{\leqslant} i\ensuremath{\leqslant} m}$, 
$b_n=(b_{k,n})_{1\ensuremath{\leqslant} k\ensuremath{\leqslant} p}$, and
$b_n^*=(b_{k,n}^*)_{1\ensuremath{\leqslant} k\ensuremath{\leqslant} p}$. Then, for every $n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb N}$,
we have
\begin{align}
&\hskip -5mm (\forall i\in\{1,\ldots,m\})\quad
a_{i,n}=(\nabla h_i+\gamma_n\partial\varphi_i)^{-1}\bigg(\nabla
h_i(x_{i,n})-\gamma_n\sum_{k=1}^pL_{ki}^*y_{k,n}^*\bigg)\nonumber\\
&\Leftrightarrow (\forall i\in\{1,\ldots,m\})\quad 
\nabla h_i(x_{i,n})-\gamma_n\sum_{k=1}^pL_{ki}^*y_{k,n}^*
\in\nabla h_i(a_{i,n})+\gamma_n\partial\varphi_i(a_{i,n})
\nonumber\\
&\Leftrightarrow\nabla h(x_n)-\gamma_nL^*y_n^*
\in\nabla h(a_n)+\gamma_nAa_n\nonumber\\
&\Leftrightarrow a_n=(\nabla h+\gamma_nA)^{-1}\big(\nabla h(x_n)
-\gamma_nL^*y_n^*\big).
\end{align}
Likewise,
\begin{equation}
(\forall n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb N})\quad 
b_n=(\nabla j+\mu_nB)^{-1}\big(\nabla j(Lx_n)+\mu_ny_n^*\big).
\end{equation}
Thus, \eqref{4eKKnhf74g203} is a special case of 
\eqref{IVe:Bfg+uh4f9-09h}. In addition, it follows from our
assumptions and \eqref{4e:funct1} that $f$, $g^*$, $h$, and $j$ 
satisfy Condition~\ref{IVC:1}, and that $\nabla h$ and $\nabla j$ 
are uniformly continuous on every bounded subset of $\ensuremath{\text{\rm int\,dom}\,} h$ 
and $\ensuremath{\text{\rm int\,dom}\,} j$, respectively. Altogether, the conclusions follow
from Theorem~\ref{IVt:1}\ref{IVt:1iv}, with 
$\overline{x}=(\overline{x}_i)_{1\ensuremath{\leqslant} i\ensuremath{\leqslant} m}$ and
$\overline{y}^*=(\overline{y}_k^*)_{1\ensuremath{\leqslant} k\ensuremath{\leqslant} p}$.
\end{proof}

Denote by $\ensuremath{{\mathcal X}}$ and $\ensuremath{{\mathcal Y}}$ the standard vector product spaces 
$\ensuremath{\raisebox{-0.5mm}{\mbox{\huge{$\times$}}}}_{\!\!i=1}^{\!\!m}\ensuremath{{\mathcal X}}_i$ and 
$\ensuremath{\raisebox{-0.5mm}{\mbox{\huge{$\times$}}}}_{\!\!k=1}^{\!\!p}\ensuremath{{\mathcal Y}}_k$ equipped with the norms 
$x=(x_i)_{1\ensuremath{\leqslant} i\ensuremath{\leqslant} m}\mapsto\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^m\|x_i\|^2}$ and 
$y=(y_k)_{1\ensuremath{\leqslant} k\ensuremath{\leqslant} p}\mapsto\sqrt{\sum_{k=1}^p\|y_k\|^2}$,
respectively. Then $\ensuremath{{\mathcal X}}^*$ is the vector product space 
$\ensuremath{\raisebox{-0.5mm}{\mbox{\huge{$\times$}}}}_{\!\!i=1}^{\!\!m}\ensuremath{{\mathcal X}}_i^*$ equipped with the norm 
$x^*\mapsto\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^m\|x_i^*\|^2}$ 
and $\ensuremath{{\mathcal Y}}^*$ is the vector product space 
$\ensuremath{\raisebox{-0.5mm}{\mbox{\huge{$\times$}}}}_{\!\!k=1}^{\!\!p}\ensuremath{{\mathcal Y}}_k^*$ equipped with the norm 
$y^*\mapsto\sqrt{\sum_{k=1}^p\|y_k^*\|^2}$. 
Let us introduce the operators
\begin{equation}
\label{4e:opt1}
\begin{cases}
A\colon\ensuremath{{\mathcal X}}\to 2^{\ensuremath{{\mathcal X}}^*}\colon x\mapsto
\ensuremath{\raisebox{-0.5mm}{\mbox{\huge{$\times$}}}}_{\!\!i=1}^{\!\!m}\partial\varphi_i(x_i)\\
B\colon\ensuremath{{\mathcal Y}}\to 2^{\ensuremath{{\mathcal Y}}^*}\colon y
\mapsto\ensuremath{\raisebox{-0.5mm}{\mbox{\huge{$\times$}}}}_{\!\!k=1}^{\!\!p}\partial\psi_k(y_k)\\
L\colon\ensuremath{{\mathcal X}}\to\ensuremath{{\mathcal Y}}\colon x\mapsto
\big(\sum_{i=1}^mL_{ki}x_i\big)_{1\ensuremath{\leqslant} k\ensuremath{\leqslant} p}
\end{cases}
\end{equation}
and the functions
\begin{equation}
\label{4e:funct1}
\begin{cases}
f\colon\ensuremath{{\mathcal X}}\to\ensuremath{\left]-\infty,+\infty\right]}\colon x\mapsto\sum_{i=1}^mf_i(x_i)\\
h\colon\ensuremath{{\mathcal X}}\to\ensuremath{\left]-\infty,+\infty\right]}\colon x\mapsto\sum_{i=1}^mh_i(x_i)\\
\varphi\colon\ensuremath{{\mathcal X}}\to\ensuremath{\left]-\infty,+\infty\right]}\colon x\mapsto\sum_{i=1}^m\varphi_i(x_i)\\
g\colon\ensuremath{{\mathcal Y}}\to\ensuremath{\left]-\infty,+\infty\right]}\colon y\mapsto\sum_{k=1}^pg_k(y_k)\\
j\colon\ensuremath{{\mathcal Y}}\to\ensuremath{\left]-\infty,+\infty\right]}\colon y\mapsto\sum_{k=1}^pj_k(y_k).
\end{cases}
\end{equation}
Then it follows from \cite[Theorem~3.1.11]{IVZali02} that $A$ 
and $B$ are maximally monotone. In addition, the adjoint of $L$ is 
$L^*\colon\ensuremath{{\mathcal Y}}^*\to\ensuremath{{\mathcal X}}^*\colon y^*\mapsto(\sum_{k=1}^p
L_{ki}^*y_k^*)_{1\ensuremath{\leqslant} i\ensuremath{\leqslant} m}$, and, as in
Proposition~\ref{pvb8uh4504}\ref{pvb8uh4504i},
$f$ and $g$ are Legendre functions. 
Thus, Problem~\ref{IVpb:V3} is a special case of 
Problem~\ref{prob:1}. Furthermore, $h$ and $j$ are Legendre
functions,
\begin{equation}
\label{ekIuh711a}
\ensuremath{\text{\rm int\,dom}\,} f=\underset{i=1}{\overset{m}{\ensuremath{\raisebox{-0.5mm}{\mbox{\huge{$\times$}}}}}}\ensuremath{\text{\rm int}\,}\ensuremath{\text{\rm dom}\,} f_i\subset
\underset{i=1}{\overset{m}{\ensuremath{\raisebox{-0.5mm}{\mbox{\huge{$\times$}}}}}}\ensuremath{\text{\rm int}\,}\ensuremath{\text{\rm dom}\,} h_i=\ensuremath{\text{\rm int\,dom}\,} h,
\end{equation}
and 
\begin{equation}
\label{ekIuh711b}
L\big(\ensuremath{\text{\rm int\,dom}\,} f\big)=\underset{k=1}{\overset{p}{\ensuremath{\raisebox{-0.5mm}{\mbox{\huge{$\times$}}}}}}
\sum_{i=1}^m L_{ki}(\ensuremath{\text{\rm int\,dom}\,} f_i)\subset
\underset{k=1}{\overset{p}{\ensuremath{\raisebox{-0.5mm}{\mbox{\huge{$\times$}}}}}}\ensuremath{\text{\rm int}\,}\ensuremath{\text{\rm dom}\,} j_k=\ensuremath{\text{\rm int\,dom}\,} j.
\end{equation}
Next we observe that, for every $i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$, since 
$h_i+\varepsilon\varphi_i$ is supercoercive, 
$(h_i+\varepsilon\varphi_i)^*$ is bounded above on
every bounded subset of $\ensuremath{{\mathcal X}}_i^*$ \cite[Theorem~3.3]{Ccm01}.
As a result, 
$(h+\varepsilon\varphi)^*\colon x^*\mapsto\sum_{i=1}^m
(h_i+\varepsilon\varphi_i)^*(x_i^*)$ 
is bounded above on every bounded subset of $\ensuremath{{\mathcal X}}^*$, and it follows
from \cite[Theorem~3.3]{Ccm01} that $h+\varepsilon\varphi$ is
supercoercive. In turn since, as in \eqref{ehHg7yG10a},
$\ensuremath{{\varnothing}}\neq\ensuremath{\text{\rm dom}\,} A\cap\ensuremath{\text{\rm int\,dom}\,} f\subset
\ensuremath{\text{\rm dom}\,}\varphi\cap\ensuremath{\text{\rm int\,dom}\,} f$, we derive from 
\cite[Theorem~2.8.3]{IVZali02}
and Lemma~\ref{l:20}\ref{l:20iii} that
\begin{equation}
\label{ekIuh713}
\nabla h+\varepsilon A=\nabla h+\varepsilon\partial\varphi=
\partial(h+\varepsilon\varphi) 
\end{equation}
is coercive. We show in a similar fashion that $\nabla j+\delta B$ 
is coercive. Now set, for every $n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb N}$, 
$a_n=(a_{i,n})_{1\ensuremath{\leqslant} i\ensuremath{\leqslant} m}$, 
$a_n^*=(a_{i,n}^*)_{1\ensuremath{\leqslant} i\ensuremath{\leqslant} m}$, 
$b_n=(b_{k,n})_{1\ensuremath{\leqslant} k\ensuremath{\leqslant} p}$, and
$b_n^*=(b_{k,n}^*)_{1\ensuremath{\leqslant} k\ensuremath{\leqslant} p}$. Then, for every $n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb N}$,
we have
\begin{align}
&\hskip -5mm (\forall i\in\{1,\ldots,m\})\quad
a_{i,n}=(\nabla h_i+\gamma_n\partial\varphi_i)^{-1}\bigg(\nabla
h_i(x_{i,n})-\gamma_n\sum_{k=1}^pL_{ki}^*y_{k,n}^*\bigg)\nonumber\\
&\Leftrightarrow (\forall i\in\{1,\ldots,m\})\quad 
\nabla h_i(x_{i,n})-\gamma_n\sum_{k=1}^pL_{ki}^*y_{k,n}^*
\in\nabla h_i(a_{i,n})+\gamma_n\partial\varphi_i(a_{i,n})
\nonumber\\
&\Leftrightarrow\nabla h(x_n)-\gamma_nL^*y_n^*
\in\nabla h(a_n)+\gamma_nAa_n\nonumber\\
&\Leftrightarrow a_n=(\nabla h+\gamma_nA)^{-1}\big(\nabla h(x_n)
-\gamma_nL^*y_n^*\big).
\end{align}
Likewise,
\begin{equation}
(\forall n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb N})\quad 
b_n=(\nabla j+\mu_nB)^{-1}\big(\nabla j(Lx_n)+\mu_ny_n^*\big).
\end{equation}
Thus, \eqref{4eKKnhf74g203} is a special case of 
\eqref{IVe:Bfg+uh4f9-09h}. In addition, it follows from our
assumptions and \eqref{4e:funct1} that $f$, $g^*$, $h$, and $j$ 
satisfy Condition~\ref{IVC:1}, and that $\nabla h$ and $\nabla j$ 
are uniformly continuous on every bounded subset of $\ensuremath{\text{\rm int\,dom}\,} h$ 
and $\ensuremath{\text{\rm int\,dom}\,} j$, respectively. Altogether, the conclusions follow
from Theorem~\ref{IVt:1}\ref{IVt:1iv}, with 
$\overline{x}=(\overline{x}_i)_{1\ensuremath{\leqslant} i\ensuremath{\leqslant} m}$ and
$\overline{y}^*=(\overline{y}_k^*)_{1\ensuremath{\leqslant} k\ensuremath{\leqslant} p}$.

Let $\ensuremath{{\mathcal X}}$ be a finite-dimensional real Banach space and let
$f\in\Gamma_0(\ensuremath{{\mathcal X}})$ be a Legendre function. Then the following
hold:
\begin{enumerate}
\item
\label{lkIuh727i--}
$f$ and $\nabla f$ are continuous on $\ensuremath{\text{\rm int\,dom}\,} f$
{\rm \cite[Corollaries~8.30(iii),~17.34, and~17.35]{Livre1}}.
\item
\label{lkIuh727i-}
$\nabla f\colon\ensuremath{\text{\rm int\,dom}\,} f\to\ensuremath{\text{\rm int\,dom}\,} f^*$ is bijective with inverse
$\nabla f^*\colon\ensuremath{\text{\rm int\,dom}\,} f^*\to\ensuremath{\text{\rm int\,dom}\,} f$
{\rm \cite[Theorem~5.10]{Ccm01}}.
\item
\label{lkIuh727i}
Let $x\in\ensuremath{\text{\rm int\,dom}\,} f$, let $y\in\overline{\ensuremath{\text{\rm dom}\,}}f$, and let 
$(y_n)_{n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb N}}\in(\ensuremath{\text{\rm int\,dom}\,} f)^{\ensuremath{\mathbb N}}$. Suppose that $y_n\to y$
and that $(D^f(x,y_n))_{n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb N}}$ is bounded. Then $y\in\ensuremath{\text{\rm int\,dom}\,} f$
and $D^f(y,y_n)\to 0$ {\rm \cite[Theorem~3.8(ii)]{BB97}}.
\item
\label{lkIuh727ii}
Let $x\in\ensuremath{\text{\rm int\,dom}\,} f$, let $y\in\ensuremath{\text{\rm int\,dom}\,} f$, let 
$(x_n)_{n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb N}}\in(\ensuremath{\text{\rm dom}\,} f)^{\ensuremath{\mathbb N}}$, and let
$(y_n)_{n\in\ensuremath{\mathbb N}}\in(\ensuremath{\text{\rm int\,dom}\,} f)^{\ensuremath{\mathbb N}}$. Suppose that 
$D^f(x_n,y_n)\to 0$. Then $x=y$
{\rm \cite[Theorem~3.9(iii)]{BB97}}.
\item
\label{lkIuh727iii}
Let $y\in\ensuremath{\text{\rm int\,dom}\,} f$. Then $D^f(\cdot,y)$ is coercive
{\rm \cite[Lemma~7.3(v)]{Ccm01}}.
\item
\label{lkIuh727iv}
Let $\{x,y\}\subset\ensuremath{\text{\rm int\,dom}\,} f$. Then 
$D^f(x,y)=D^{f^*}(\nabla f(y),\nabla f(x))$
{\rm \cite[Lemma~7.3(vii)]{Ccm01}}.
\end{enumerate}
